study.title: Jeremiah 14 - Dry, confession, judgment, and hope in the God who sends the rain
study.overview: Jeremiah 14 presents a drought crisis that at the same time exposes the fragility of the land and the spiritual gravity of Judah. The chapter alternates between description of suffering, confession of sin, divine warning, denunciation of false prophets, and a final prayer based on the unique character of the LORD. The drought does not appear only as an agricultural problem: it becomes a sign that the people live in rebellion, that external religiosity does not solve sin, and that only the God of Israel has the power to sustain creation and, therefore, is the only hope of his people.

outline.title: The land in mourning because of drought
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the drought reaching Judah in full: weakened doors, Jerusalem's crying, empty cisterns, ashamed farmers, suffering animals and the breeding itself groaning for lack of water and pasture.

outline.title: Confession of the people and cry for help
outline.explanation: The people recognize their wickedness and appeal to the name of the LORD, calling him hope and redeemer. The prayer, however, mixes confession with a request for presence, as if God were distant, and asks him not to abandon the community that bears his name.

outline.title: Divine answer: judgment, prophetic falsehood and mourning of the prophet
outline.explanation: God rejects intercession in behalf of a people who insist on evil, proclaim judgment by sword, famine and pestilence, and exposes the prophets who promised peace without divine mandate. Jeremiah laments the ruin of the people and describes a situation without leaving, with death in both the countryside and the city.

outline.title: New confession and appeal to God that rains
outline.explanation: The people recognize personal and inherited guilt, they ask that God do not dishonor his throne or revoke his covenant, and concludes by stating that idols cannot give rain. Only the Lord rules nature, so hope must rest in it.

study.context: The chapter is presented as the word of the LORD given to Jeremiah in the midst of a severe drought that affects Judah and Jerusalem. The notes indicate that the crisis was so serious that the reservoirs dried up and the population suffered a threat of starvation. Matthew Henry understands that this trial took place at the end of Josiah's reign and the beginning of Jehoiakim's, as a warning for larger judgments; Adam Clarke notes that there is no certain historical record of a specific drought, but points out that the region was naturally vulnerable to long periods without rain. These observations help to place the text as a response to a real calamity, without the chapter relying on additional historical details for its main meaning.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that creation is under the rule of God and that the rain does not belong to idols or human powers, but to the Creator. The drought works as judgment and as a revelation: it shows the emptiness of material security, the insufficiency of sacrifices without repentance and the falsehood of a religion that wants blessing without submission. The text also highlights the seriousness of collective sin, the responsibility of religious leaders and God's fidelity to his own covenant, even though this fidelity includes severe discipline. At the same time, the final prayer reveals that true hope is not in human merits, but on the name, throne and covenant of the LORD.

scholarViews.insight: The drought reached the economic and domestic life of Judah: the reservoirs dried up, lacked water to drink and cook, and the cry came up from Jerusalem.
The confession of the people appears without real abandonment of sin; they try to move God through religious appeals, but they continue in iniquity.
Only the true God can rain; idols are useless before God's rule over nature.

questions: What changes when we understand that material scarcity can reveal a deeper spiritual crisis?
How can we fall into the error of confessing guilt without abandoning, in fact, sin?
Is our practical trust in the Lord that makes it rain, or in substitutes who promise security but cannot sustain life?
study.practice: This chapter calls the community of faith to unite sincere repentance and humble hope. Instead of treating God as an automatic solution to crises, the believer is invited to examine his life, confess real sins, reject deceitful religious voices, and wait in the LORD as the only source of sustenance. In practice, this means praying with sincerity, obeying with readiness, discerning teachings that promise peace without conversion and remember that even material needs depend on God's provision.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not allow you to safely state which specific historical drought is in view, or detail the exact dates of the event. Nor is there enough basis to accurately identify all the institutional mechanisms of the prophets mentioned, in addition to what the notes themselves say. The interpretations of Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke should be read as devotional and explanatory readings, not as undisputed conclusions of the text.
